passage:
Dear Lalit bhaiya,
You asked about my school project, "A Day I'll Never Forget", so here's mine: the day the cyclone reached our town two years ago. I remember it perfectly. I was in the science lab when the siren went off, the windows rattled, and Mr Das told us to get under the tables. I even remember the smell of the burner.
But when I showed my draft to Papa, he said the schools were shut that day. Dadi laughed. "My boy, you were at home eating my laddoos." I argued. Then Dadi found the old school notice: closed for two days.
I'm still shocked. I was SO sure. Maybe I mixed it up with the fire drill we had later?
Anyway, I'm rewriting it with Dadi's version.
Your cousin, Chaitanya

qa.q: What did the old school notice say?
qa.a: It said the school was closed for two days.

qa.q: Why was Chaitanya so sure about being in the science lab?
qa.a: The day was so frightening that the memory felt sharp, down to the burner smell, and that strong feeling made him confident even though pieces like the later fire drill may have mixed in.

qa.q: What choice did Chaitanya make after seeing the notice?
qa.a: He chose to rewrite the project with Dadi's version, trusting the record over his feeling of certainty.

qa.q: How might Lalit bhaiya react to this letter?
qa.a: Lalit may be surprised too, and might start wondering about his own vivid memories of the cyclone day.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy who is very sure where he was during a frightening event, though the details had drifted.

passage:
Binita, you want my story for the school radio? Okay. For me it's the night of the blackout, when the whole city went dark for two days. I was thirteen, which makes me a very dramatic boy of fifteen now.
I remember it like a film. I was at my uncle's shop, counting coins, when the lights died. A man shouted, a dog howled, and I ran home through black streets holding a candle.
Last week I told my mum, and she said, "Divyansh, you were at home. We found the candles together in the kitchen drawer." My cousin says the howling dog was at his house.
I'm still sure about the running. I can feel it in my legs. But maybe my memory is a story I've told too many times.

qa.q: Where did Divyansh's mum say he was when the lights went out?
qa.a: She said he was at home, and they found the candles together in the kitchen drawer.

qa.q: Why does Divyansh still feel sure about running home?
qa.a: The night was frightening and dramatic, so the memory feels vivid, even physical, like something he can feel in his legs.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do before telling the story on the radio?
qa.a: He could say "this is how I remember it" and include his mum's version, so listeners hear that memories drift.

qa.q: How might his mum feel hearing Divyansh's dramatic version?
qa.a: She may be amused, or a little sad that he doesn't remember finding the candles with her, a moment that mattered to her.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy who is very sure where he was during a citywide shock, though his family remembers it differently.

passage:
I'm Asif, Karthik's classmate. On Monday in history, sir asked about the day the earthquake shook our district three years ago. Karthik's hand shot up. "I was at the bus stop. The shelter swayed, a coconut fell, and a woman dropped her tiffin. It was 7:40."
He sounded so sure that half the class went quiet.
The thing is, I was with him that morning. We were in my house playing carrom when the glasses rattled. We ran out together.
After class I told him. He looked at me as if I'd said the sky was green. "No, I remember the coconut."
I don't know what's in his head. Maybe the bus stop was someone else's story. He's still not sure he believes me.

qa.q: What were Asif and Karthik playing when the glasses rattled?
qa.a: They were playing carrom in Asif's house.

qa.q: Why did Karthik answer so confidently in history?
qa.a: The shock of that day left a vivid picture, with the time, the coconut and the tiffin, so it feels exact to him even though Asif remembers it differently.

qa.q: How could Karthik and Asif find out whose memory is right?
qa.a: They could ask family members or look for messages from that morning, instead of relying on how sure each of them feels.

qa.q: What is it like for Asif to contradict a friend who seems so certain?
qa.a: Asif probably feels awkward, being looked at as if he'd said the sky was green, and admits he cannot know what is in Karthik's head.

grounding: It shows a classmate noticing a teenage boy's vivid, confident memory of an earthquake morning that does not match what happened.

passage:
Friday night: The ground shook at 9:40. Rustam, fifteen, was brushing his teeth, green toothbrush in hand, when Jasleen screamed from the hall. He ran out with foam on his chin. The whole Jalandhar building stood in the street, whispering.
Next Thursday: At school, everyone told their "where were you" story. Rustam said, "I was in the kitchen holding a steel glass of water. It shook right in my hand." He could almost feel it.
Three months later: For English he wrote an essay called "When the Earth Moved." It opened on the stairs, one foot on the landing, a glass in hand. Jasleen read it at the dining table and put her finger on the first line. "Veerji, you came out of the bathroom with toothpaste on your face." He shook his head, completely sure. "No. I remember the glass."

qa.q: What was Rustam holding when the shaking began on Friday night?
qa.a: He was brushing his teeth with a green toothbrush in hand.

qa.q: Why did Rustam stay completely sure about the glass even when Jasleen disagreed?
qa.a: The fright made the memory feel sharp and vivid, and each time he retold it the new detail felt more real, so his confidence stayed high while the facts drifted.

qa.q: When could Rustam have noticed his memory changing, and what would help him check it?
qa.a: The essay was a good moment to pause; comparing it with what Jasleen and the family recall, or anything written that week, would show how details had shifted.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel about her brother's version of that night?
qa.a: She may be amused or frustrated, since she clearly saw him with toothpaste on his face and cannot understand why he is so sure of the glass.

grounding: Across three days, a teenage boy's memory of a frightening earthquake shifts in details while his confidence stays strong.

passage: Come, Gargi, sit. You asked what the cyclone was like. I was sixteen. For fifty years I have told everyone the same thing: I was on the jetty at Machilipatnam with my father, wearing my yellow shirt, tying our boat as the wind tore the tin roof off the net shed. I can see that yellow shirt now, wet and flapping. Last year Neelam, my school friend, visited. "You were at our house," Neelam said. "We sat under the table listening to the radio." I laughed and argued. Then your Nani found a letter I had written to my cousin that very week. It said, "We are safe at Neelam's house." My own handwriting, beta. And still, close my eyes, and I am on that jetty. Strange, how sure a frightened heart can be.

qa.q: What did the letter Nani found say?
qa.a: It said, "We are safe at Neelam's house," in the narrator's own handwriting.

qa.q: Why does the narrator still feel they were on the jetty, even after seeing the letter?
qa.a: The cyclone was so frightening that the memory feels vivid and certain, and fifty years of retelling it has made the jetty picture feel like the truth.

qa.q: What did the narrator choose to do once the letter turned up, and why is that wise?
qa.a: The narrator accepted their own handwriting over the picture in their head while still admitting the jetty feels real; holding both lets the memory matter without being treated as proof.

qa.q: How might Neelam have felt hearing the jetty story told for so long?
qa.a: Neelam might have been puzzled or amused, remembering clearly that they both sat under a table listening to the radio.

grounding: An elder recalls how they were certain for decades about where they were during a cyclone as a teenager, though a letter showed otherwise.
